content: English can put a spotlight on one part
of a sentence by splitting it in two.
Plain: "The session changed everything."
Spotlight the subject:
"It was the session that changed
everything."
The frame is always the same:
it + be + the part you want + that/who.
"It was in June that they met."
"It was John who paid."
"It is the noise that I mind, not the
hours."
Use it to correct or to insist:
"It wasn't me who told her."
Many languages move the word itself, or
add a particle, to mark the focus;
English builds a whole second clause
around it.
A second way to aim the spotlight, this
time forward:
what + clause + is/was + the point.
"What I need is a week off."
"What annoys me is the noise."
"What he did was sell the whole lot."
The new information lands at the END,
where English likes to keep it.
Fronting moves a part to the FRONT for
contrast instead:
"That I can believe."
"Stubborn he certainly is."
"The rest we can discuss later."
The two tools pull opposite ways. The
what-cleft saves the news till last;
fronting throws the contrasted part
out in front.
Many languages reorder freely because
endings show who does what; English has
few endings, so it builds these frames.
Put a negative word first and the
sentence inverts like a question.
"Never had I seen anything like it."
not "Never I had seen ..."
"Not only was the report brief, it was
wrong."
"No sooner had she left than it rang."
The pattern: negative adverbial, then
helper, then subject.
"Little did she know."
"Under no circumstances should you sign."
"Rarely do we see such weather."
"Not until Monday did they reply."
If there is no helper, do steps in:
"Rarely DO we see ..."
This is formal and emphatic — a tool for
writing and speeches, not for chat.
Many languages lift the voice or add a
particle for this weight; English turns
the word order over instead.
